claim: Winding-up orders
requested_remedy: Winding-up orders
parties: Plaintiff: Petitioner, represented by Miss Pauline Lo of Director of Legal Aid
Defendant: BG Lighting Company Limited and BG International Limited

facts.F1: BG Lighting Company Limited (Lighting) and BG International Limited (International) are related companies
facts.F2: The first petition was presented on 4 January 2000 against Lighting based on a Labour Tribunal award for arrears of wages of approximately $270,000
facts.F3: The second petition was presented on 12 January 2000 against International also based on a Labour Tribunal award of approximately $32,000
facts.F4: Both companies were represented by their common director, Mr Wong Pak Sum
facts.F5: The two petitions were heard together and winding-up orders were made at the hearing on 22 May 2000
facts.F6: On 10 January 2000, Horwath Corporate Solutions Limited (Horwath) was appointed as the independent financial adviser of Lighting and the Group to formulate a restructuring plan
facts.F7: At the hearing on 20 March 2000, Mr Wong informed the court that Horwath would present a restructuring proposal to the board as soon as possible
facts.F8: However, there was no evidence of any progress having been made, and Lighting was granted an adjournment of four weeks
facts.F9: Lighting did not engage solicitors due to lack of financial resources
facts.F10: On 14 April 2000, Mr Wong filed written submissions on behalf of Lighting seeking dismissal of the petition
facts.F11: A draft letter from Horwath dated 10 April 2000 stated that the management accounts for the years ended 31 March 1999 and 2000 were expected to be available before 30 April 2000 and 22 May 2000, respectively
facts.F12: Horwath anticipated presenting the restructuring plan by mid-June 2000
facts.F13: A list of creditors showed the Group's indebtedness to be of the order of $46.4 million
facts.F14: On 17 April 2000, the Group was represented by another director, Madam Fu Yuk Sum, who sought a further adjournment
facts.F15: The Group was told that unless a viable restructuring plan with the necessary in-principle support was before the court on 15 May 2000, it faced the prospect of winding-up orders
facts.F16: At the hearing on 15 May 2000, no restructuring plan was before the court, and the Group was given one last opportunity to place the requisite evidence before the court
facts.F17: At the hearing on 22 May 2000, the Group produced letters from a number of its creditors, whose debts in the aggregate amounted to some $31.6 million, and a letter from Horwath stating that it was unable to proceed with the formulation of the restructuring plan due to the unavailability of financial statements
facts.F18: The letter also stated that no restructuring would be viable without an immediate injection of capital of at least $2 million, and there was no evidence of any potential investor willing to consider a capital injection
facts.F19: The financial statements were not available due to the circumstances beyond the Group's control
facts.F20: The court considered that the presentation of a winding-up petition triggers the Protection of Wages on Insolvency Fund Board's discretion

reference_issues: Whether a further adjournment was warranted given the Group's failure to present a viable restructuring plan
authorities:
The Companies Ordinance, Cap.32
Protection of Wages on Insolvency Ordinance
relevant_cases: In re UDL Holdings Limited HCMP 436 of 1999

facts.F1: On 8 December 1999, the plaintiff's board of directors held a meeting which was attended by Mr Lam Sai Fat, Mr Chin Luen Cheong and Mr Chan Tak in which it was resolved that the plaintiff would make a loan in the total sum of HK$1,518,595.29 to its shareholders in equal portions of HK$379,648.82 each.
facts.F2: The validity of the board resolution is not challenged by the Claimant.
facts.F3: On 15 September 2000, the Claimant filed a petition in HCCW No. 850 of 2000 seeking minority shareholder's relief under Section 168A of the Companies Ordinance, Cap. 32 against the Plaintiff, Mr Lam Sai Fat, Mr Chin and Mr Lam Wai Hong.
facts.F4: A meeting of the directors was subsequently held on 26 January 2000 and an extraordinary general meeting on 21 February 2000.
facts.F5: The Claimant was absent from both meetings and he challenged the validity of the resolutions in those meetings.
facts.F6: The Claimant also claimed that in July 2000 he was wrongfully removed as a signatory to the Plaintiff's bank account and that sums of money had been withdrawn from the Plaintiff's bank account subsequently without his knowledge or consent.
facts.F7: On 18 September 2000, the Defendant received a letter from the Claimant's solicitors enclosing a copy of the petition and requesting the Defendant not to release the money held by the Defendant as stakeholder to anyone without a court order in view of the petition.
facts.F8: On 20 September 2000, the Defendant wrote to the Plaintiff's solicitors advising them of the letter from the Claimant's solicitors and stating that the Defendant would not release the money held as stakeholder unless and until the Plaintiff had obtained an order from the court for that purpose.
facts.F9: On 23 December 2000, the Claimant filed a notice to act in person in the winding-up proceedings and in the present proceedings.

facts.F11: The petition was dismissed for want of prosecution on 2 January 2001.

facts.F1: The Applicant is a 35-year-old national of Bangladesh who last arrived in Hong Kong on 25 May 2018 with permission to continue to work as a foreign domestic helper until the expiration of her employment contract on 25 May 2020 or within 14 days of its early termination.
facts.F2: When her employment was prematurely terminated on 31 July 2018, she did not depart and instead overstayed.
facts.F3: More than one year later on 30 October 2019, she surrendered to the Immigration Department and raised a non-refoulement claim on the basis that if she returned to Bangladesh, she would be harmed or killed by the family of her deceased husband over some land dispute in her home village.
facts.F4: The Applicant was born and raised in Joypurhat, Bangladesh.
facts.F5: After leaving school, she was arranged by her family to marry her much older husband, who was a farmer and owned lands and properties jointly with his several brothers in the village.
facts.F6: After the marriage, the Applicant moved to live with her husband in his home and subsequently gave birth to their daughter.
facts.F7: Three years later, her husband met an accident and became paralyzed, and eventually passed away in mid-2007.
facts.F8: Soon, the brothers of her deceased husband demanded the Applicant and her daughter to leave the property, and when she refused, they started to threaten and harass her, and eventually, she and her daughter had no choice but to return to her mother’s home.
facts.F9: To make her living and to support her daughter, the Applicant worked in a garment factory, and in 2014, she started to come to Hong Kong to work as a foreign domestic helper.
facts.F10: After her last employment was terminated in 2018, she was afraid to return to Bangladesh and overstayed in Hong Kong.
facts.F11: She subsequently raised her non-refoulement claim for protection and completed a Non-refoulement Claim Form (“NCF”) on 21 January 2020 and attended a screening interview before the Immigration Department with legal representation from the Duty Lawyer Service (“DLS”).
facts.F12: By a Notice of Decision dated 17 March 2020, the Director of Immigration rejected the Applicant’s claim on all applicable grounds.
facts.F13: On 27 March 2020, the Applicant lodged an appeal to the Torture Claims Appeal Board against the Director’s decision.
facts.F14: On 18 May 2022, her appeal was dismissed by the Board, which also confirmed the Director’s decision.
facts.F15: On 6 June 2022, the Applicant filed her Form 86 for leave to apply for judicial review of the Board’s decision.
facts.F16: The Court has determined that the Applicant could relocate to another part of Bangladesh where she would not face the alleged risk of harm.
facts.F17: The Applicant has since resolved her problem and now wants to return to her home country, as stated in her recent affirmation requesting to withdraw her application.

claim: Application for leave to apply for judicial review of the decision of the Director of Immigration dated 14 December 2021 (the “Director’s Decision”) refusing her subsequent claim of HCAL 2887 of 2018 (the “previous claim”) under section 37ZO of the Immigration Ordinance, Cap. 115
requested_remedy: Application for leave to apply for judicial review of the decision of the Director of Immigration dated 14 December 2021 (the “Director’s Decision”) refusing her subsequent claim of HCAL 2887 of 2018 (the “previous claim”) under section 37ZO of the Immigration Ordinance, Cap. 115

facts.F1: The applicant is an illegal immigrant from the Philippines and came to Hong Kong as a domestic helper.
facts.F2: Her employment was terminated and she overstayed after her last employment in Hong Kong.
facts.F3: On 5 April 2017, she surrendered to the Immigration Department.
facts.F4: On 4 and 25 August 2017, she lodged non-refoulement claim on the grounds of Torture risk under Part VIIC of the Ordinance; BOR 3 risk under Article 3 of the Bill of Rights Ordinance; Persecution risk under the Refugee Convention and BOR 2 risk, Right to Life under Article 2 of the Bill of Rights Ordinance.
facts.F5: Her claim on all applicable risks was rejected by the Director by a Notice of Decision dated 12 February 2018.
facts.F6: She appealed to the Torture Claims Appeal Board (the “Board”). By its Decision dated 2 October 2018 (the “Board’s Decision”), the Board dismissed her appeal on all claims.
facts.F7: She applied for leave for judicial review of the Board’s Decision and her application was dismissed by the Court of the First Instance on 19 July 2019 (the “Court’s Order”).
facts.F8: Her application for appeal against the Court’s Order to the Court of Appeal was dismissed by the Court of Appeal on 2 December 2019.
facts.F9: Her notice of motion for leave to appeal the Court of Appeal’s decision to the Court of Final Appeal was dismissed by the Court of Appeal on 4 June 2020.
facts.F10: Her application for leave to appeal to the Court of Final Appeal was dismissed by the Court of Final Appeal on 28 July 2021.
facts.F11: She applied to the Director for making a subsequent claim by letter of 3 August 2021.
facts.F12: The factual basis of her previous claim is that if refouled, she will be harmed or killed by her ex-boyfriend, Jonathan Agoban in domestic violence and she is in fear of her father because she was traumatized by his loss of interest and trust on her.
facts.F13: The Director found that her claim was not substantiated and her conduct was inconsistent with the imminence of threats as she alleged.
facts.F14: The Director also found that her father’s behaviour does not amount to minimum level of severity and his mere disapproval of her relationship with Jonathan does not warrant non-refoulement protection.
facts.F15: State protection would be available to her and internal relocation was a viable alternative.
facts.F16: The Board affirmed the Director’s Decision and found that the state was not involved in the incidents and it can provide protection to her.
facts.F17: The applicant said that one of her sisters told her that Jonathan and his friends had killed Egick, the boyfriend of her sister, Sunshine due to a dispute between them, and she is worried that Jonathan may harm her if she returns to the Philippines.
facts.F18: The Director has considered the additional information but did not accept that there is significant change of circumstances and such information, coupled with the previous claim, would not give her subsequent claim any realistic prospect of success.
facts.F19: The applicant is at risk of making further applications to assert her non-refoulement claim on the same facts, thereby abusing the legal process.

facts.F1: The two parties are the main contractor and a sub-contractor in relation to a project
facts.F2: Disputes between the parties have already arisen and have been referred to arbitration pursuant to an arbitration clause in the sub-contract between the two parties
facts.F3: The arbitration is due to be heard in early August and is scheduled to last two weeks
facts.F4: On 29 June, the Plaintiff issued the present Writ against the Defendant
facts.F5: The Acknowledgment of Service was filed on 9 July
facts.F6: On the same day, the Defendant took out a summons for stay pursuant to the provisions in the Arbitration Ordinance and pursuant to an arbitration clause in the sub-contract

facts.F8: The Plaintiff has twice applied for leave to amend its claims under the arbitration proceedings to include the present court dispute as part of the disputes in the arbitration proceedings for the resolution of the arbitrator
facts.F9: The two applications were successfully opposed by the Defendant on the ground that the disputes go outside the existing scope of disputes under the two arbitration notices and on the ground that the amendments were not properly formulated
facts.F10: The Plaintiff's counsel has been acting for the Plaintiff for several years in the related arbitration proceedings
facts.F11: The Plaintiff's counsel is familiar with the disputes between the parties
facts.F12: The Plaintiff has already had counsel in the related arbitration proceedings who must be well familiar with the disputes between the parties and who must be competent enough to give whatever advice that is required at short notice relating to the present dispute
facts.F13: No affidavit has been filed by the Plaintiff in opposition to the present application

claim: winding-up orders for the four companies due to debts incurred since 1996
requested_remedy: winding-up orders for the four companies due to debts incurred since 1996
parties: Defendant: NHD Systems (Holdings) Limited, NHD Systems (Asia) Limited, Siu-Fung Ceramics Holdings Limited, Siu-Fung Ceramics Concept Company Limited, and Mr Lee Siu Fung

facts.F1: The four companies belong to the same group, known as the Siu Fung Group.
facts.F2: The debts which brought about these Petitions were incurred since about 1996.
facts.F3: The Petitions themselves were issued over a year ago in April 1999.
facts.F4: The evidence discloses that the Petitions have been adjourned to await the outcome of a restructuring proposal made to the body of creditors earlier.
facts.F5: By mid-April 2000, it became clear that such proposal was not accepted by all the creditors.
facts.F6: Four restructuring proposals are being put forward now.
facts.F7: The Petitioner, together with Heng Sang Bank Limited and HSBC Private Equity, are creditors whose debts constitute about 60% of the total indebtedness of the Siu Fung Ceramics Holdings Limited.
facts.F8: They are not agreeable to any of the 4 proposals.
facts.F9: Apart from Mr Lee, no other creditors have indicated that they wish to consider the new proposals.
facts.F10: The court relied on the evidence before it to determine the Petitioner's interest in having a winding-up ordered.
facts.F11: The court considered the history of the proceedings and the lack of agreement from the major creditors.

reference_issues: Whether the companies should be wound up due to their inability to pay their debts.
Whether the Petitioner has sufficient interest in having a winding-up ordered.
Whether Siu Fung Ceramics Concept Company Limited has sufficient connection with Hong Kong.
authorities:
The Companies Ordinance (Cap.32)
French: Applications to Wind Up Companies (1993)
relevant_cases:
Re Chapel House Colliery Company (1883) 24 Ch D 259
Re UDL Holdings Limited [1999] 3 HKC 210

facts.F1: The issue to be decided is whether to give a direction that all affidavits or affirmations filed on behalf of the Secretary for Justice shall stand as the evidence in chief of the deponents at the trial of these committal proceedings provided that the deponents do attend the trial to be cross-examined on their affidavits or affirmations by the respondents
facts.F2: A total of 17 applications were heard together
facts.F3: The background facts to these proceedings are well known to the parties
facts.F4: The Court of Appeal in Secretary for Justice v Cheung Kai Yin [2014] 4 HKLRD 367 confirmed that the Rules of the High Court are generally applicable to proceedings for criminal contempt
facts.F5: A similar direction was given in the Taxi Cases by consent
facts.F6: The trial process will permit the deponents to adopt their affidavits or affirmations as their evidence in chief
facts.F7: The deponents are required to attend the trial to be cross-examined on their affidavits or affirmations by the respondents
facts.F8: No particular prejudice will be suffered by the respondents as a result of the direction
